title: Generated IDs and Identity Columns Across DBMS Products
learningObjectives: Explain how SQLite INTEGER PRIMARY KEY generates row identifiers.
Distinguish SQLite AUTOINCREMENT from ordinary INTEGER PRIMARY KEY behaviour.
Recognize AUTO_INCREMENT, IDENTITY and GENERATED AS IDENTITY in other DBMS products.
Explain why generated IDs can contain gaps.
Avoid using generated identifiers as gap-free business sequence numbers.

understand.concept: Database products provide different ways to generate unique row identifiers. SQLite commonly uses INTEGER PRIMARY KEY as an alias for the rowid; AUTOINCREMENT changes reuse behaviour and has additional overhead. Other DBMS products use identity or sequence features with different syntax.
understand.whyItMatters: Correct identity design avoids collisions, understands gaps and supports reliable relationships and insert workflows.
understand.analogy: SQL portability is like translating a precise instruction into several product dialects: the intent stays the same, but the exact words and rules can differ.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not model type systems, function return types, time-zone rules, optimizer behaviour or transaction semantics.

explain.narrative:
## SQLite generated row identifiers
In an ordinary SQLite rowid table, an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY column aliases the rowid and receives a generated integer when omitted. AUTOINCREMENT prevents reuse of previously issued rowids in specific circumstances but adds overhead; it is not required for ordinary generated IDs.

## Other database products
MySQL commonly uses AUTO_INCREMENT, SQL Server uses IDENTITY, and PostgreSQL supports GENERATED AS IDENTITY as well as sequences. The syntax, retrieval APIs and transactional behaviour differ.

## Gaps and assumptions
Generated identifiers are unique keys, not gap-free business numbers. Failed inserts, deletes and concurrency can create gaps. Do not use an identity column as a count of transactions or as a guaranteed chronological business sequence.

AUTOINCREMENT is not required for normal generated IDs.

Use a separate business-numbering process if gap-free numbering is legally required.

questions.prompt: What does SQLite INTEGER PRIMARY KEY do in a rowid table?
options: Aliases the rowid and can generate an integer when omitted
Prevents all deleted IDs from being reused in every case
questions.answer: Aliases the rowid and can generate an integer when omitted
questions.explanation: INTEGER PRIMARY KEY aliases the rowid and can generate values.

questions.prompt: Is AUTOINCREMENT required for ordinary generated IDs in SQLite?
questions.explanation: INTEGER PRIMARY KEY already generates values; AUTOINCREMENT adds specific non-reuse behaviour and overhead.

questions.prompt: Which keyword is common for MySQL generated integer IDs?
Which feature is commonly used by SQL Server?
questions.explanation: SQL Server uses IDENTITY columns for generated values.

questions.prompt: Should an identity column be treated as a gap-free invoice number?
options: No, generated identifiers can contain gaps
Yes, every generated ID is consecutive forever
Only when a table has a foreign key
questions.answer: No, generated identifiers can contain gaps
questions.explanation: Identity values are keys, not guaranteed gap-free business sequences.
